title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
hook: night three closes the clearing nights: the gods are offered a boon, and ask for something you can use again

segments.voice: Yesterday was night two of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Durga, hard to pass, and the boat across. Tonight, night three.

Choose a boon. The path heard the goddess say it to the gods earlier this year, reading the Devi Mahatmya whole. The buffalo demon is dead, and the gods could ask for anything: riches, safety forever, a share of her power. Tonight is night three, the last of the clearing nights that, in one way of counting, belong to Durga. And that old request, from the end of the fourth chapter, comes back with a new job. Inside a nine-night course, it's a lesson about coming back.
screen: `CHOOSE A BOON.` → `HEARD BEFORE.` → `NOW, A LESSON ABOUT COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's their answer, in paraphrase. Everything has already been done for us, they say, because our enemy is dead. But if you'll give us a boon, then whenever we remember you again, destroy our worst troubles. And be gracious to anyone who praises you with these hymns. The goddess agrees, and vanishes. Look at what they didn't ask for: not a fortress that would last forever, not a guarantee that nothing bad would happen again. As if they know it will. Heaven has been lost once; it can be lost twice. So they ask for something you can use again. Not a single rescue, but a promise of return: remember me, and I'll come. That's what makes it the right close for the first stretch. Clearing isn't a chore done once and crossed off a list. The road fills up again: clutter, worries, the same old anger. What the first nights teach is not a final cleanup but a way of returning, the habit of remembering the one who clears. Some devotees take the line literally: in trouble, they recite these chapters, or simply say the goddess's name. Others read it inwardly: the remembering is itself the clearing, the moment a person stops and turns toward something larger than the mess in front of them. And it widens the circle. The gods don't ask only for themselves, but for anyone who sings these hymns. Three nights in, the first lesson is learned: what clears the road once can be called on again.
screen: `OUR ENEMY IS ALREADY DEAD.` · `WHENEVER WE REMEMBER YOU, COME.` · `NOT ONE RESCUE, A WAY OF RETURN.` · `FOR ANYONE WHO SINGS THESE HYMNS.` · then, large: `WHAT CLEARS THE ROAD CAN BE CALLED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that has crowded your road these three nights, a worry, a task, a grudge, and on an out-breath let it be set to one side, just for now, noticing the little room it leaves. Then think of what you'd turn to when it comes back: a name, a person, a breath like this one. If you pray, you can say the goddess's name, or the name you use, once, as the remembering; if you don't, let the breath be what you return to.
Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Night three closes the clearing nights, with the gods' boon: whenever we remember you, come.

fork.setup: it's night three, and the clearing nights are ending. the road will fill up again. what does the gods' boon suggest you carry into the next nights?
options: a promise that nothing will block the road again.
a way of returning: something to remember when it fills up.
a plan to stop clearing altogether.
fork.reveal: the gods don't ask for a road that stays clear. they ask that whenever they remember her, she destroy their worst troubles: a way of returning.

original.note: Sanskrit vara: a boon, a gift chosen by the one who receives it.

chat.says: If the demon was already dead, what did the gods even ask the goddess for?
options: A way back: whenever they remember her again, she'd come and clear their worst troubles.
A fortress in heaven so strong that no demon could ever attack them again.
A share of her power, so they'd never have to call on her again.
